title: Graphing Artifact: False Vertical Risers in the Step Function
originalTopic: Connecting-mode artifacts when plotting discontinuous functions
author: Muhammad Abdullah Athar
problemStatement: When y = floor(x), the greatest-integer function, is plotted in the usual connected-line mode, the screen shows vertical line segments at every integer in addition to horizontal steps. Explain what those segments are, and describe the true graph.
finalAnswer: \lfloor x \rfloor = n \ \text{for } n \le x < n + 1; \quad \text{the true graph is a staircase with no vertical segments}

steps.title: Write the function piece by piece
steps.mathExpression: f(x) = n \quad \text{on} \quad [n, n+1), \qquad f(n) = n, \quad \lim_{x \to n^-} f(x) = n - 1
steps.explanation: On each half-open interval of length 1 the output is constant, and at each integer the value jumps up by exactly 1.
steps.why: The definition itself says the function never takes the intermediate values between n - 1 and n, so no vertical piece can belong to the graph.

steps.title: Identify the source of the artifact
steps.explanation: Sampling at or near consecutive integers produces two points whose y-values differ by 1; the connecting mode draws a straight segment between them, which appears as a riser at x = n plus a slanted trace.
steps.why: Graphing software interpolates linearly between adjacent samples and does not test whether the function is continuous there, so the segment is a rendering choice, not a mathematical fact.

steps.title: Correct the display
steps.mathExpression: \text{unplug mode / separate segments } y = n \text{ on } [n, n+1) \text{ with closed left, open right endpoint}
steps.explanation: Switching to point mode, plotting each constant piece separately, or restricting the domain to a single interval removes the risers and leaves horizontal treads with a filled dot at the left end and an open dot at the right end.
steps.why: Only endpoint conventions can express the jump, because a single connected stroke cannot represent a function with jump discontinuities.

steps.title: Generalize the lesson
steps.explanation: The apparent thickness and slope of the false risers change with the window size and sample count, while the genuine staircase never changes.
steps.why: A feature that varies with plotting settings but not with the function is diagnostic of an artifact rather than mathematics.
